newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel approves interim nuclear storage dump.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel approves interim nuclear storage dump.

text.p: A Senate panel Thursday passed a bill to build a temporary dump in Nevada for radioactive waste from nuclear power reactors, but the Clinton administration has threatened to veto the measure.

The Senate Energy Committee voted 15-5 in favour of the bill which calls for having a site ready in 1999 in the Nevada desert to start accepting waste that is accumulating near nuclear plants across the country.

Committee Chairman Frank Murkowski, the Alaska Republican who sponsored the bill, said it was safer to have a central dump than to have waste at more than 70 sites, some of which are running out of space.
He also said the government is obligated by law to start taking control of the waste next year, but will not have a permanent repository ready to accept it for another 15 years.
But the Clinton administration has said the bill would make Nevada the nation's nuclear dump without a thorough review, and it would divert resources from building the permanent repository.
The only site under consideration for a permanent dump is Yucca Mountain in Nevada, but the administration has not completed reviews of the site.

The committee rejected several amendments offered by New Mexico Democrat Jeff Bingaman to extend construction deadlines, limit the facility's capacity and increase environmental reviews of the proposed waste dump.

Bingaman said as the bill was written, if the administration decided not to go forward with the permanent repository in Yucca Mountain, "The defacto result is putting the waste on a cement pad in Nevada and then we're telling Nevada it's up to them to decide how to get rid of it."
But Murkowski said the government must have a way to dispose of the waste to avoid massive lawsuits from utilities, which have paid some $12 billion into a fund to build a central facility.
The Senate passed Murkowski's bill last year, but with four fewer votes than the two-thirds majority needed to override Clinton's threatened veto.
Nevada's two Democratic senators, staunch opponents of the measure, have said they still expect to have the votes to sustain a presidential veto.

"It's not a surprise that the committee passed it. We've always remained focused on the floor vote and we remain confident that we have the votes to sustain a veto, which we are sure would come," a spokeswoman for Sen. Harry Reid said.
